top.text: Kahlo soon began a relationship with Rivera, who was 21 years her senior and had two common-law wives. Kahlo and Rivera were married in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Coyoacán on 21 August 1929. Her mother opposed the marriage, and both parents referred to it as a "marriage between an elephant and a dove", referring to the couple's differences in size; Rivera was tall and overweight while Kahlo was petite and fragile. Regardless, her father approved of Rivera, who was wealthy and therefore able to support Kahlo, who could not work and had to receive expensive medical treatment. The wedding was reported by the Mexican and international press, and the marriage was subject to constant media attention in Mexico in the following years, with articles referring to the couple as simply "Diego and Frida".

answer: The Amazon rainforest is being cut down primarily due to human activities like cattle farming and soybean farming[1]. Furthermore, tropical rain forests in the Amazon Basin are being cut down at an unsustainable rate, which leads to serious environmental problems[2]. Loggers cut down large trees, and the remaining vegetation is often burned to supply nutrients for other plants, a process that continues as more forest is cleared[2]. Human settlement and land development are also main sources of deforestation in the Amazon[4].

While Alexander Graham Bell is often credited with being the first to transmit articulate speech using undulatory currents of electricity[2], there has been significant dispute regarding who deserves recognition as the first inventor[1][3]. Antonio Meucci is supported by some scholars as a real inventor, although others outside of Italy do not recognize the claims that his device influenced the development of the telephone[2]. The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World; ) is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor. The copper-clad statue, a gift to the United States from the people of France, was designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.
The statue is a figure of a classically draped woman, inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas. She holds a torch above her head with her right hand, and in her left hand carries a tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI (July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals), the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. With her left foot she steps on a broken chain and shackle, commemorating the national abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.

Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor. He is known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system.
Born and raised in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Tesla first studied engineering and physics in the 1870s without receiving a degree. He then gained practical experience in the early 1880s working in telephony and at Continental Edison in the new electric power industry. In 1884, he migrated to the United States, where he became a naturalized citizen. He worked for a short time at the Edison Machine Works in New York City before he struck out on his own. With the help of partners to finance and market his ideas, Tesla set up laboratories and companies in New York to develop a range of electrical and mechanical devices. His AC induction motor and related polyphase AC patents, licensed by Westinghouse Electric in 1888, earned him a considerable amount of money and became the cornerstone of the polyphase system, which Westinghouse marketed.

history.answer: Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, with a smaller effect from the Sun.

answer: Tides are the regular rising and falling of sea levels caused mainly by the gravitational attraction from the Moon and the Sun[1][2][3][4]. As the Earth rotates on its axis, areas directly in line with the Moon experience high tides, resulting in two high tides and two low tides each tidal day[1]. These periodic rises and falls are a result of the differential gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun, combined with inertial effects related to the Earth–Moon system's orbital motion[2]. While the Moon is the primary driver, the Sun's tidal forces also substantially modulate oceanic tides[3]. Furthermore, actual observed tides are modified by terrestrial factors such as the geometry of ocean basins, continental boundaries, bathymetry, and the Coriolis effect[2]. During each tidal cycle, water rises to a maximum height called "high tide" before receding to a minimum "low tide" level, which exposes more of the foreshore known as the intertidal zone[4].

history.answer: The Cold War was a period of geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, from about 1947 to 1991.

answer: The Cold War was a period of international geopolitical rivalry between the United States (US) and the Soviet Union (USSR) and their respective allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and the communist Eastern Bloc[1][2]. This tension occurred after World War II[4][5]. The term "cold war" is used because there was no direct military fighting between the two superpowers, but they each supported opposing sides in regional conflicts known as proxy wars[1][2]. A cold war is defined as a state of conflict between nations that avoids direct military action but focuses on economic and political actions, propaganda, espionage, or proxy wars waged by surrogates[3]. This rivalry involved campaigns, embargoes, and sports diplomacy[1]. The Cold War lasted almost half a century and ultimately determined the future of the global network following World War II[4].

history.answer: Plants grow by making food through photosynthesis and by cell division at growing tips called meristems.

answer:
Plants grow through a combination of cell growth and cell division[3]. This growth occurs in special tissues called meristems; root apical meristems grow downward into the soil, while shoot apical meristems grow upward[1].

For plants to grow, several requirements must be met:
*   **Energy and Food:** Plant growth needs glucose produced by photosynthesis and energy generated through respiration[2]. Plants obtain their energy from sunlight using a green pigment, as they are predominantly photosynthetic or descended from photosynthetic ancestors[5].
*   **Minerals:** Growth also requires minerals that are obtained from the soil[2].
*   **Hormones:** Plant growth is controlled by plant hormones known as auxins[2].
*   **Water:** Plants continuously absorb and release water, which allows for normal growth and development; this process involves osmosis, where water moves from areas of high potential to low potential in the soil[6].

Furthermore, plants grow by accumulating scattered pieces of their environment and assembling them into an organic entity, which is an extraordinary phenomenon[4]. Plants generally increase in both size and weight as they grow[4].

top.text:
Plants are the eukaryotic organisms that constitute the kingdom Plantae . They are predominantly photosynthetic or came from photosynthetic ancestors, meaning that they obtain their energy from sunlight by using the green pigment chlorophyll in their chloroplasts to produce sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Over the course of time, some plants have evolved to be parasitic, meaning they take energy from other organisms. Except for glaucophytes, some green algae and a few red algae, most plants are multicellular.
Historically, as in Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom encompassed all living things that were not animals, and included algae and fungi. Definitions have narrowed since then; current definitions exclude fungi and some of the algae. By the definition used in this article, plants form the clade Viridiplantae (green plants), which consists of the green algae and the embryophytes or land plants (hornworts, liverworts, mosses, lycophytes, ferns, conifers and other gymnosperms, and flowering plants). A definition based on genomes includes the Viridiplantae, along with the red algae and the glaucophytes, in the clade Archaeplastida.

history.answer: DNA is the molecule that carries the genetic instructions of living things. It is a double helix of two strands.

answer:
DNA, which stands for deoxyribonucleic acid, is a molecule that carries the genetic instructions necessary for the growth, development, functioning, and reproduction of all known living organisms and many viruses[4]. It is a nucleic acid composed of a long chain of linear polymers that contain deoxyribose sugars covalently bonded to bases known as nucleic acids[1][3].

Key details about DNA include:
*   **Structure:** DNA is shaped like a double helix[5].
*   **Function:** Its major function is the storage of genetic information[1][3].
*   **Building Blocks:** DNA is made up of nucleotides, which serve as the building blocks of life[2].
*   **Coding:** In DNA, a sequence of three bases called a codon is responsible for encoding a single amino acid[1][3].
*   **Genes:** The segments of DNA that carry genetic information are referred to as genes, although other DNA sequences have structural purposes or are involved in regulating the use of this information[6].

DNA is one of the three major types of macromolecules essential for all known forms of life, alongside proteins and complex carbohydrates[4].

top.text:
Deoxyribonucleic acid (; DNA) is a polymer composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix. The polymer carries genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses. DNA and ribonucleic acid (RNA) are nucleic acids. Alongside proteins, lipids and complex carbohydrates (polysaccharides), nucleic acids are one of the four major types of macromolecules that are essential for all known forms of life.
The two DNA strands are known as polynucleotides as they are composed of simpler monomeric units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide is composed of one of four nitrogen-containing nucleobases (cytosine [C], guanine [G], adenine [A] or thymine [T]), a sugar called deoxyribose, and a phosphate group. The nucleotides are joined to one another in a chain by covalent bonds (known as the phosphodiester linkage) between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, resulting in an alternating sugar-phosphate backbone. The nitrogenous bases of the two separate polynucleotide strands are bound together, according to base pairing rules (A with T and C with G), with hydrogen bonds to make double-stranded DNA. The complementary nitrogenous bases are divided into two groups, the single-ringed pyrimidines and the double-ringed purines. In DNA, the pyrimidines are thymine and cytosine; the purines are adenine and guanine.

answer: The Silk Road was a network of historical trade routes across Asia connecting China to Europe[4]. It is not a single road but rather an intricate web of land and sea routes that spanned from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century[1][4]. The name "Silk Road" originates from the lucrative trade in silk textiles, which were primarily produced in China[2][3]. This network began with the expansion of the Han dynasty into Central Asia around 114 BCE, facilitated by the explorations and missions of the Chinese imperial envoy Zhang Qian[2]. By the first century CE, Chinese silk became highly desired in regions such as Rome, Egypt, and Greece[2]. The name itself derives from the German term *Seidenstraße*, which was popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen through his seven expeditions to China[3]. Some historians prefer the term "Silk Routes" because it more accurately describes the extensive web of routes connecting Central, East, South, Southeast, and West Asia, as well as East Africa and Southern Europe[1].

top.text: The Great Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. Spanning over 6400 km (4,000 mi) on land, it played a central role in facilitating economic, cultural, political, and religious interactions between the Eastern and Western worlds. The name "Silk Road" was coined in the late 19th century, but some 20th- and 21st-century historians instead prefer the term Silk Routes, on the grounds that it more accurately describes the intricate web of land and sea routes connecting Central, East, South, Southeast, and West Asia as well as East Africa and Southern Europe. In fact, some scholars criticise or even dismiss the idea of silk roads and call for a new definition or alternate term. According to them, the literature using this term has "privileged the sedentary and literate empires at either end of Eurasia" thereby ignoring the contributions of steppe nomads. In addition, the classic definition sidelines prominent civilisations such as India and Iran.

Dolphins are carnivorous cetaceans, while sharks are a different class of fish. Dolphins are marine mammals that are closely related to whales and porpoises[6]. They are characterized by being aquatic mammals with a beak-like snout and are famed for their intelligence[2]. Dolphins are widespread in pelagic marine environments but some species inhabit brackish or freshwater bodies, preferring warm tropical waters, although some, like the right whale dolphin, prefer colder climates[3].

Regarding differences in terms of predators, most smaller dolphin species face risks from a few larger sharks, such as the bull shark, dusky shark, tiger shark, and great white shark, particularly for calves[4]. However, some larger dolphin species, like orcas, may prey on smaller dolphins, though this is rare[3][4]. query: How does it compare to the French Revolution?

history.query: When did the American Revolution happen?
history.answer: The American Revolution took place from 1765 to 1791, and the Revolutionary War was fought from 1775 to 1783.

answer:
The American and French Revolutions were ideologically and politically different movements. The American Revolution primarily focused on achieving independence from colonial domination, whereas the French Revolution aimed for a complete overhaul of French society, which included overturning an existing monarchy[4].

Key differences between the two are as follows:
*   **Focus:** The American Revolution was mainly about freeing the colonies from British rule[4]. In contrast, the French Revolution targeted a thorough transformation of French society, including replacing what was already a failing monarchy[4].
*   **Ideological Impact:** The American Revolution influenced the French Revolution both politically and ideologically[4]. The ideas from the American Revolution are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy[1].
*   **Timeline Context:** The American Revolution spanned from 1765 to 1789, leading to the Constitution taking effect in 1789 and the Bill of Rights being ratified in 1791[2]. The French Revolution began with the Estates General on May 5, 1789, and concluded with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on November 9, 1799[1][5].
*   **Political Division:** After the Americans gained independence, political divisions in the U.S. were seen as minor compared to the violent polarization between the left and right that began with the French Revolution in 1789[3].

answer: Yes, Austrian German is distinct from the German spoken in Germany. Austrian German, also known as Standard Austrian German (ASG), Standard Austrian German (Österreichisches Standarddeutsch), or simply Austrian (Österreichisch), is a variety of Standard German used in Austria and South Tyrol[2]. This variety is considered separate from the version spoken in Germany or Switzerland due to German's pluricentric nature[4]. While both are related, they have different customs and cultures, and Austrians maintain a distinct national identity separate from Germans[5].

history.answer: The internet is a global network of computer networks that exchange data using a shared set of rules, the Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP). Data is split into small packets, each labeled with the address of its destination. Routers pass the packets from network to network until they reach that address, where they are put back together; packets from one message may take different paths. Every device on the internet has an IP address, and the Domain Name System (DNS) translates names such as wikipedia.org into these addresses. Internet service providers connect homes and businesses, and they are linked by high-capacity backbone cables, including undersea fiber-optic cables. Services such as the World Wide Web and email run on top of this network.

history.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria turn light energy into chemical energy. In plants it takes place mainly in the leaves, inside chloroplasts that contain the green pigment chlorophyll. In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll absorbs sunlight, and the energy is used to split water molecules, which releases oxygen and produces the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, the plant uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide from the air into sugars such as glucose. The overall reaction turns six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water into one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen. Photosynthesis supplies most of the oxygen in the air and the energy for nearly all food chains.

Essentially, it is a chemical process where plants use sunlight to change carbon dioxide into sugars, which serve as energy for the cell[3]. This process involves capturing the energy from light using a pigment called chlorophyll[6]. The captured light energy is then used to create glucose, which is a form of chemical energy that the organism can later release to fuel its activities[4][6].

top.text: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration. Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

history.query: What caused the fall of the Roman Empire?
history.answer: Historians name many causes for the fall of the Western Roman Empire, which is usually dated to 476, when the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer. Politically, the empire suffered from civil wars, frequent coups and weak emperors, especially during the crisis of the third century. Economically, heavy taxes, inflation from debased coins and shrinking trade weakened it. The army relied more and more on Germanic soldiers and allies whose loyalty was uncertain. From the late fourth century, migrating peoples such as the Goths, Vandals and Huns put pressure on the borders, and the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. The split of the empire into eastern and western halves also left the poorer West to defend itself, while the Eastern Empire survived until 1453.

history.answer: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it passes the boundary called the event horizon. Black holes form when very massive stars collapse at the end of their lives, and supermassive black holes with millions to billions of solar masses sit at the centres of most large galaxies, including the Milky Way. A black hole cannot be seen directly, but astronomers detect it from its effects: the orbits of nearby stars, the glowing disk of hot gas that spirals into it, and gravitational waves when two black holes merge. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.

history.query: How does a nuclear reactor work?
history.answer: A nuclear reactor produces heat by splitting atoms in a controlled chain reaction. The fuel is usually uranium enriched in uranium-235, formed into pellets and packed into fuel rods. When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it splits into smaller nuclei, releases a large amount of energy as heat, and frees two or three more neutrons that can split other nuclei. A moderator, often water, slows the neutrons so they cause more fissions, and control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials such as boron are moved in or out to keep the reaction steady. The heat boils water, directly or through a heat exchanger, and the steam spins a turbine connected to a generator. Thick shielding and a containment building keep the radiation inside.

answer:
A nuclear reactor works by safely managing a controlled chain reaction of atomic fission to produce energy. In simpler terms, the device is designed to carry out nuclear reactions in a regulated and controlled way[3]. It stabilizes this process by regulating neutron absorbers and moderators within the core[5]. To operate it, water flows through the reactor core to collect the heat generated from the nuclear fission[4][5].

The sources explain that a nuclear reactor is a device used to sustain a controlled fission chain reaction[5]. The fuel is typically arranged in several hundred vertical rods[4], and control rods are used to shut the reactor down by absorbing neutrons; operators move these rods up gradually to start it[4]. The heat from this fission is then passed to a working fluid coolant, which in commercial reactors drives turbines and electrical generator shafts[5].

top.text:
A nuclear reactor is a device used to sustain a controlled fission nuclear chain reaction. They are used for commercial electricity, marine propulsion, weapons production, and research. Fissile nuclei (primarily uranium-235 or plutonium-239) absorb single neutrons and split, releasing energy and multiple neutrons, which can induce further fission. Reactors stabilize this, regulating neutron absorbers and moderators in the core. Fuel efficiency is exceptionally high; low-enriched uranium is 120,000 times more energy-dense than coal.
Heat from nuclear fission is passed to a working fluid coolant. In commercial reactors, this drives turbines and electrical generator shafts. Some reactors are used for district heating, and isotope production for medical and industrial use.

history.answer: The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945, after the Second World War, to maintain international peace and security and to promote cooperation between countries. It has 193 member states. Its main bodies include the General Assembly, where every member has a vote, and the Security Council, whose five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, can veto its resolutions. The Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General, runs its daily work, and the International Court of Justice settles disputes between states. Its headquarters are in New York City. Specialized agencies and programmes, such as the World Health Organization and UNICEF, work on health, food, children, refugees and development.

The United Nations (UN) is an international intergovernmental organization established by the signing of the Charter of the United Nations on 26 June 1945 with the articulated mission of maintaining international peace and security, to develop friendly relations among states, to promote international cooperation, and to serve as a centre for harmonizing the actions of states in achieving those goals.
The United Nations headquarters is located in New York City, with several other offices located in Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and The Hague. The UN comprises six principal organizations: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, International Court of Justice, Secretariat and Trusteeship Council which, together with several specialized agencies and related agencies, make up the UN System. There is a total of 193 member states, representing nearly all of the world's sovereign states, as well as two observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine.
